# Fractals and scaling {#sec-fractals-and-scaling}

Many objects that complex systems produce have no characteristic size. A coastline, a branching aggregate of particles or a
strange attractor shows new detail at every magnification, and the sizes of cities, the frequencies of words and the
fluctuations of a river level spread over many orders of magnitude without a typical value. The common language of these
observations is scaling: a quantity changes by a fixed factor when the scale of observation changes by a fixed factor, and the
exponent that relates the two factors is the number worth measuring. For a geometric object this exponent is a fractal
dimension; for a distribution it is the exponent of a power law; for a time series it is the Hurst exponent; for an organism
or a city it is an allometric exponent. This chapter defines these exponents, proves the results that make them meaningful,
and computes them on models and samples. The power-law tails of @def-heavy-tail and the strange attractors of
@def-strange-attractor are the starting points: the first gives the distributions whose exponents are estimated here, the
second the sets whose dimensions are measured.

The chapter follows the scaling chapter of @thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018 [Ch. 3], the benchmark of the subject, with
@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017 [Secs. 3.1-3.6, 4.5 and App. B] for aggregation, fractal geometry and power-law
fits, @downeyThinkComplexity2018 [Chs. 4 and 7] for heavy tails and box counting, @datserisNonlinearDynamicsConcise2022
[Secs. 5.3-5.4] and @dilaoDynamicalSystemChaos2023 [Secs. 5.2 and 5.4] for the dimensions of attractors and for iterated
function systems, @lindgrenInformationTheoryComplex2024 [Sec. 6.2] for the resolution-dependent dimension,
@jensenComplexityScienceStudy2023 [Secs. 10.3-10.4] for correlations in time and the Hurst exponent, and
@clauset2009power for the statistics of power laws. The analysis it rests on (geometric series, continuity, the contraction
mapping theorem, maximum likelihood and the limit theorems) is in the mathematics tutorial, in
[Real analysis](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/real-analysis/index.qmd#sec-series),
[Sets, relations and topology](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/sets-relations-topology/index.qmd#sec-metric-spaces)
and [Probability](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#sec-statistics), and is linked
rather than restated.

The chapter has six sections. @sec-self-similarity-dimension defines the box-counting dimension, proves that a self-similar set
satisfying the open set condition has the dimension given by its similarity ratios, and defines the correlation and
generalised dimensions of attractors and measures. @sec-fractal-growth defines diffusion-limited aggregation and the mass
dimension of a growing cluster. @sec-scaling-laws proves that scale invariance forces a power law, defines Zipf's law, and
proves that sample-space-reducing processes produce it. @sec-measuring-power-laws proves the properties of the
maximum-likelihood estimator of a power-law exponent and defines the test of Clauset, Shalizi and Newman.
@sec-scaling-in-time defines the Hurst exponent and proves how it follows from the correlations of the increments.
@sec-allometric-scaling defines allometric and urban scaling laws and proves the three-quarter law of the model of West, Brown
and Enquist. Critical phenomena, the other great source of scaling, need the theory of phase transitions and are not treated
here.

Following the conventions of the tutorial, fractal dimensions always carry an index ($D_0$, $D_2$, $D_q$, $D_f$), the
exponent of a power-law density $p(x) \propto x^{-\alpha}$ is $\alpha$, and $\bar F(x) = \mathbb P(X > x)$ is the complementary
distribution function. Every definition, proposition and theorem is followed by ten examples and ten exercises, each exercise
with a hidden solution in two tabs: the argument, then a computation with its recorded output. The computations use
scikit-complexity 0.9.0. The systems come from its catalogue: `CantorSetSystem`, `KochCurveSystem`,
`SierpinskiSubstitutionSystem`, `ChaosGameSystem`, `HenonMapSystem`, `LorenzSystem`, `LogisticMapSystem`,
`DiffusionLimitedAggregationSystem`, `SampleSpaceReducingSystem`, `SimonYuleSystem`, `RandomTypewritingSystem`,
`MandelbrotLeastEffortSystem`, `ExponentialGrowthAtRandomTimesSystem`, `KestenProcessSystem`, `MultiplicativeProcessSystem`,
`FractionalBrownianMotionSystem`, `WestBrownEnquistSystem` and `GravityUrbanScalingSystem`. They are run by `simulate` and
analysed with `scaling` (box counting, correlation dimension, detrended fluctuations, rescaled range, allometric fits),
`fit_law` (the method of Clauset, Shalizi and Newman, through the powerlaw package), `distribution` (the Hill estimator and
complementary distributions) and `lyapunov`. NumPy and SciPy are used for closed formulas, for exact enumerations and for
drawing samples of known laws.

## Self-similarity and fractal dimension {#sec-self-similarity-dimension}

A dimension is a scaling exponent. Doubling the side of a square multiplies its area by $2^2$, doubling the edge of a cube
multiplies its volume by $2^3$, and the exponent is the dimension [@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 3.5.2.1, eq.
(3.49)]. Sets such as the Koch curve, built by replacing each piece by smaller copies of the whole, answer the same question
with an exponent that is not an integer, and so do the attractors of chaotic maps. This section turns the question into a
definition that can be computed from a picture or a sample, the box-counting dimension, proves that for exactly
self-similar sets it equals the exponent read off the construction, and then defines the dimensions of a distribution of
points, which are what one measures on an attractor. Sets of fractal dimension come back
later in the chapter, as aggregates of particles and as the branching networks of organisms.

For more on this topic, see @thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018 [Secs. 3.5.1-3.5.2], @charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017
[Secs. 3.5-3.6], @downeyThinkComplexity2018 [Ch. 7], @datserisNonlinearDynamicsConcise2022 [Secs. 5.3-5.4],
@dilaoDynamicalSystemChaos2023 [Secs. 5.2 and 5.4] and @lindgrenInformationTheoryComplex2024 [Sec. 6.2].

### Box counting

To measure the size of a set at resolution $\varepsilon$, cover it with a grid of cubes of side $\varepsilon$ and count the
cubes it meets. For a curve the count grows like $\varepsilon^{-1}$, for a surface like $\varepsilon^{-2}$, and the exponent of
the growth is taken as the dimension [@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 3.5.2.2, eq. (3.51);
@datserisNonlinearDynamicsConcise2022, Sec. 5.4]. The definition keeps only this count and forgets everything else about the
set: two sets with the same counts at all small scales have the same dimension, whatever their topology. Since the limit need
not exist, the definition records the lower and upper limits as well.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-box-counting-dimension}
#### Box-counting dimension

Let $A \subset \mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and bounded. For $\varepsilon > 0$, let $N(\varepsilon)$ be the number of the cubes
$[k_1\varepsilon, (k_1 + 1)\varepsilon) \times \dots \times [k_n\varepsilon, (k_n + 1)\varepsilon)$, $k_i \in \mathbb Z$, that
meet $A$. The **lower** and **upper box-counting dimensions** of $A$ are
$$
\underline D_0(A) = \liminf_{\varepsilon \to 0}\frac{\log N(\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\varepsilon)} ,\qquad
\overline D_0(A) = \limsup_{\varepsilon \to 0}\frac{\log N(\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\varepsilon)} .
$$
If they are equal, their common value is the **box-counting dimension** $D_0(A)$, so that $N(\varepsilon) =
\varepsilon^{-D_0 + o(1)}$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. A set whose box-counting dimension exists and is not an integer is called a
**fractal**.
:::

::::

Since $A$ lies in a bounded cube, $N(\varepsilon) \leq C\varepsilon^{-n}$, so $0 \leq \underline D_0 \leq \overline D_0 \leq n$.
The name fractal is used here in the computable sense of the definition; Lindgren calls a set fractal when its fractal
dimension exceeds its topological dimension, $D_T < D_F \leq D_E$ in his notation, which also covers curves of integer
dimension above one [@lindgrenInformationTheoryComplex2024, Sec. 6.2.1, eq. (6.23)]. The Hausdorff dimension, the measure-theoretic
version, agrees with $D_0$ for all the self-similar sets of this section and is not needed below.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest sets have the dimensions one expects. A finite set is zero-dimensional, because its count stops growing once the
boxes are smaller than the distances between its points.

::: {#exm-box-finite}
#### A finite set

A set of $m$ points meets at most $m$ boxes, and at least one, so $1 \leq N(\varepsilon) \leq m$ and $\log
N(\varepsilon)/\log(1/\varepsilon) \to 0$: $D_0 = 0$.
:::

A segment of the line is the model of a one-dimensional set. Its count is computed exactly, and it already shows that the
grid position changes $N(\varepsilon)$ only by a bounded factor.

::: {#exm-box-segment}
#### A segment

For $A = [0, 1] \subset \mathbb R$, the boxes $[k\varepsilon, (k + 1)\varepsilon)$ with $0 \leq k \leq \lfloor 1/\varepsilon\rfloor$
meet $A$, so $N(\varepsilon) = \lfloor 1/\varepsilon\rfloor + 1$, between $1/\varepsilon$ and $1/\varepsilon + 1$; hence $D_0 = 1$.
:::

A solid region of the plane, or any bounded set with interior points in $\mathbb R^n$, has the full dimension. The count is
squeezed between the boxes inside a small ball and those around a large one.

::: {#exm-box-open-set}
#### Sets with interior

If $A$ contains a ball of radius $a$ and lies in a cube of side $b$, then $N(\varepsilon) \geq (2a/\varepsilon - 2)^n/n^{n/2}$ for small
$\varepsilon$ (the inscribed cube of the ball, of side $2a/\sqrt n$, holds that many whole boxes) and $N(\varepsilon) \leq (b/\varepsilon +
1)^n$. Both bounds are of order $\varepsilon^{-n}$, so $D_0 = n$, the dimension of a square or a cube in Thurner's opening example.
:::

The middle-thirds Cantor set is the first fractal. It is what remains of $[0, 1]$ after removing the open middle third of every
interval again and again [@dilaoDynamicalSystemChaos2023, Sec. 4.3; @thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 3.5.2]; at the
scale $3^{-k}$ it looks like $2^k$ intervals.

::: {#exm-box-cantor}
#### The Cantor set

After $k$ steps the set lies in $2^k$ closed intervals of length $3^{-k}$, and each of them meets one or two boxes of side $3^{-k}$
(the right endpoint can spill into the next box). So $2^k \leq N(3^{-k}) \leq 2^{k + 1}$ and $D_0 = \log 2/\log 3 \approx 0.6309$,
as the exercises check on a grid. `CantorSetSystem` produces the intervals of generation $k$; it counts $2^k$ of them, of total
length $(2/3)^k$.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import CantorSetSystem
trajectory = simulate(CantorSetSystem(), until=6)
print("intervals:", trajectory.get_values("cantor.size").astype(int).tolist())
print("total length:", trajectory.get_values("cantor.length").round(4).tolist())
```

```{.text .run-output}
intervals: [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]
total length: [1.0, 0.6667, 0.4444, 0.2963, 0.1975, 0.1317, 0.0878]
```
:::

The Koch curve is built from a segment by replacing its middle third with the two other sides of an equilateral triangle, and
repeating this on every segment [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 3.5, Fig. 3.6;
@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Fig. 3.9]. @fig-koch-sierpinski shows the first generations; each one has four times as
many segments, each a third as long.

::: {#exm-box-koch}
#### The Koch curve

At the scale $3^{-k}$ the curve looks like $4^k$ segments, so $N(3^{-k})$ is of order $4^k$ and $D_0 = \log 4/\log 3 \approx 1.2619$,
which the theorem of the next unit proves. `KochCurveSystem` draws generation $k$ and rasterises it on a grid of $3^8$ cells per
side, and `scaling` of kind `'box-counting'` counts the occupied boxes. The local slopes $\log_3(N(\varepsilon)/N(3\varepsilon))$ equal
$\log 4/\log 3$ at fine scales; at coarse scales they are larger, because a box of the size of the whole curve meets it in a few boxes
whatever its dimension, and a straight fit over all scales would overestimate $D_0$.

![The first generations of the Koch curve (left) and the Sierpiński gasket drawn by the chaos game (right): every generation of the curve
replaces each segment by four segments a third as long, and the gasket is made of three copies of itself at half the size.](figures/koch_sierpinski.svg){#fig-koch-sierpinski width=95%}

```{.python .run}
import math
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import KochCurveSystem
koch = simulate(KochCurveSystem(), until=9).structures[-1]["koch"]
result = scaling(koch.get_raster(6561, bounds=(0, 0, 1, 1)), kind="box-counting", scales=[3, 9, 27, 81, 243, 729])
local = [math.log(result.counts[i] / result.counts[i + 1], 3) for i in range(5)]
print("boxes:", result.counts.astype(int).tolist())
print("local slopes, fine to coarse:", [round(v, 4) for v in local], f"log 4 / log 3 = {math.log(4, 3):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
boxes: [19732, 4932, 1233, 294, 67, 15]
local slopes, fine to coarse: [1.262, 1.2619, 1.3049, 1.3461, 1.3623] log 4 / log 3 = 1.2619
```
:::

The Sierpiński gasket keeps the three corner triangles of half the side of a triangle and repeats. Downey meets it in the
one-dimensional cellular automaton of rule 18, whose pattern of live cells has a box-counting slope of about $1.57$
[@downeyThinkComplexity2018, Ch. 7, "Fractals"].

::: {#exm-box-sierpinski}
#### The Sierpiński gasket

Generation $k$ is made of $3^k$ triangles of side $2^{-k}$, so $N(2^{-k})$ is of order $3^k$ and $D_0 = \log 3/\log 2 \approx 1.585$.
The rule-18 pattern after $2^k$ steps is the same set drawn on a lattice, which explains Downey's slope. The total area of generation
$k$ is $(3/4)^k$ times the first, so the gasket has area zero although it has infinite length.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import SierpinskiSubstitutionSystem
trajectory = simulate(SierpinskiSubstitutionSystem(), until=8)
gasket = trajectory.structures[-1]["sierpinski"]
result = scaling(gasket.get_raster(1024), kind="box-counting", scales=[2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
print("area ratio:", round(trajectory.get_values("sierpinski.area")[-1] / trajectory.get_values("sierpinski.area")[0], 5),
      "= (3/4)^8 =", round(0.75**8, 5))
print(f"box-counting slope {result.exponent:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
area ratio: 0.10011 = (3/4)^8 = 0.10011
box-counting slope 1.5532
```
:::

The dimension depends on the range of scales over which the count is read. Lindgren makes this explicit with the
resolution-dependent dimension $D(r) = -\partial\log N(r)/\partial\log r$ of a set observed at resolution $r$, and with
Mandelbrot's ball of thread [@lindgrenInformationTheoryComplex2024, Sec. 6.2.1, eqs. (6.24)-(6.25)].

::: {#exm-box-ball-of-thread}
#### The ball of thread

A ball of $10$ cm made of thread $1$ mm thick looks like a point from far away ($D(r) \approx 0$), like a solid ball at a resolution
of centimetres ($D(r) \approx 3$), like a tangle of lines at millimetres ($D(r) \approx 1$), and again three-dimensional inside a
thread. The box-counting dimension of the definition is the limit $r \to 0$, the last regime of a mathematical set; for a physical
object one reports $D(r)$ over a stated range.
:::

The length of a fractal curve measured with a yardstick $\varepsilon$ is $L(\varepsilon) = N(\varepsilon)\varepsilon$, which grows
without bound as the yardstick shrinks. This is Richardson's observation on the coast of Britain
[@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 3.5; @thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, eq. (3.52)].

::: {#exm-box-coastline}
#### The length of a coastline

If $N(\varepsilon) \approx c\varepsilon^{-D_0}$, then $L(\varepsilon) \approx c\varepsilon^{1 - D_0}$. For the west coast of Britain,
Mandelbrot found $D_0 \approx 1.25$ over a range of map scales [@lindgrenInformationTheoryComplex2024, Sec. 6.2.2], so halving the
yardstick lengthens the coast by a factor $2^{0.25} \approx 1.19$. Thurner reads the dimension of the coast of Norway from a log-log
plot of $N(\varepsilon)$ [@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Fig. 3.11].
:::

Countable sets can have positive dimension, which shows that $D_0$ measures how a set is spread out, not how many points it has. The
sequence $1/j$ is the standard example.

::: {#exm-box-harmonic-sequence}
#### The set $\{1/j\}$

For $A = \{1, \frac12, \frac13, \dots\} \cup \{0\}$ and small $\varepsilon$, the points $1/j$ with $1/j - 1/(j + 1) > \varepsilon$,
that is $j \lesssim \varepsilon^{-1/2}$, each need a box of their own, while the rest lie in $[0, \varepsilon^{1/2}]$, which
about $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ boxes cover. So $N(\varepsilon)$ is of order $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ and $D_0 = \frac12$, although $A$ is
countable and its Hausdorff dimension is $0$. An exercise makes the bounds precise.
:::

The attractors of chaotic maps are the fractals that this tutorial cares most about. The Hénon attractor of
@exm-strange-henon is covered by squares of decreasing size in @datserisNonlinearDynamicsConcise2022 [Sec. 5.4, Fig. 5.5]; the
box-counting slope comes out near $1.26$.

::: {#exm-box-henon}
#### The Hénon attractor

A long orbit of the Hénon map at $a = 1.4$, $b = 0.3$ is binned on a grid over the attractor, and the occupied cells are counted at
box sides from $2^{-6}$ to $2^{-2}$ of the window. Finite orbits fill the finest boxes only partly, which is why the smallest boxes are
left out of the fit.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.dynamical_systems import HenonMapSystem
orbit = simulate(HenonMapSystem(x=0.0, y=0.0), until=400000)
x, y = orbit.get_values("map.x")[1000:], orbit.get_values("map.y")[1000:]
grid = np.histogram2d(x, y, bins=1024, range=[[-1.5, 1.5], [-0.45, 0.45]])[0] > 0
result = scaling(grid, kind="box-counting", scales=[4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
print("boxes:", result.counts.astype(int).tolist())
print(f"box-counting slope {result.exponent:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
boxes: [2025, 863, 373, 150, 64]
box-counting slope 1.249
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes a box count by hand for a segment that does not lie along the grid. It checks that a straight line
in the plane is one-dimensional whatever its direction.

::: {#exr-box-diagonal}
#### A diagonal segment

Show that the diagonal $\{(t, t) : 0 \leq t \leq 1\}$ of the unit square has $N(\varepsilon) = \lfloor 1/\varepsilon\rfloor + 1$, and
that a segment of slope $\frac12$ and the same horizontal extent has between $1/\varepsilon$ and $2/\varepsilon + 2$ boxes. Count the
boxes on a grid.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The point $(t, t)$ lies in the box $(\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor, \lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor)$, so the diagonal meets exactly the
diagonal boxes $k = 0, \dots, \lfloor 1/\varepsilon\rfloor$. For $(t, t/2)$, the column index $\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor$ takes
$\lfloor 1/\varepsilon\rfloor + 1$ values, which gives the lower bound, and in each column the segment rises by $\varepsilon/2$, so it
meets one or two boxes there. Either way $N(\varepsilon)$ is of order $1/\varepsilon$ and $D_0 = 1$.

## Python

The two segments are sampled densely and the occupied boxes are counted at $\varepsilon = 1/64$ and $1/256$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 200001)
for eps in (1 / 64, 1 / 256):
    counts = [len({(int(a // eps), int(b // eps)) for a, b in zip(t, slope * t)}) for slope in (1.0, 0.5)]
    print(f"1/eps = {round(1 / eps)}: diagonal {counts[0]}, slope 1/2 {counts[1]}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1/eps = 64: diagonal 65, slope 1/2 65
1/eps = 256: diagonal 257, slope 1/2 257
```
::::
:::

A dimension should not depend on the position or the size of the set. The second exercise proves this for similarities, which is
what makes the dimension a property of the shape.

::: {#exr-box-similarity-invariance}
#### Invariance under similarities

Let $T(\mathbf x) = r\mathbf Q\mathbf x + \mathbf b$ with $r > 0$ and $\mathbf Q$ orthogonal. Show that $N_{T(A)}(r\varepsilon) \leq 3^n
n^{n/2}N_A(\varepsilon)$ and conclude that $T(A)$ has the same lower and upper dimensions as $A$. Check on the Sierpiński gasket
scaled by $\frac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A box of side $\varepsilon$ has diameter $\sqrt n\,\varepsilon$, so its image under $T$ has diameter $\sqrt n\,r\varepsilon$ and lies in a
cube of side $\sqrt n\,r\varepsilon$ parallel to the grid. Such a cube meets at most $(\sqrt n + 2)^n \leq 3^nn^{n/2}$ boxes of side
$r\varepsilon$ along each axis combined. Covering $T(A)$ by the images of the $N_A(\varepsilon)$ boxes gives the inequality, and the
same argument for $T^{-1}$ gives the reverse one. The constant and the factor $r$ disappear in $\log N/\log(1/\varepsilon)$.

## Python

Check on the gasket: the counts of the gasket and of its half-size copy, at boxes scaled with it, have the same slope.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import SierpinskiSubstitutionSystem
gasket = simulate(SierpinskiSubstitutionSystem(), until=8).structures[-1]["sierpinski"]
full = gasket.get_raster(1024)
half = np.zeros((2048, 2048), dtype=bool)
half[1024:, :1024] = full
a = scaling(full, kind="box-counting", scales=[2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
b = scaling(half, kind="box-counting", scales=[2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
print("counts equal:", bool((a.counts == b.counts).all()), f"slopes {a.exponent:.4f} {b.exponent:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
counts equal: True slopes 1.5532 1.5532
```
::::
:::

The limit in the definition is over all $\varepsilon$, but only a geometric sequence of scales is ever computed. The third
exercise shows that this is enough, which justifies the box sides $2^{-k}$ or $3^{-k}$ used throughout.

::: {#exr-box-geometric-scales}
#### Geometric sequences of scales suffice

Let $0 < c < 1$ and $\varepsilon_k = c^k$. Show that $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ of $\log N(\varepsilon)/\log(1/\varepsilon)$ over all
$\varepsilon \to 0$ equal those over the sequence $\varepsilon_k$. Check numerically that $N(\varepsilon)$ for the Cantor set changes
by a bounded factor between consecutive $\varepsilon_k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $\varepsilon_{k + 1} \leq \varepsilon < \varepsilon_k$, a box of side $\varepsilon_k$ meets at most $(\varepsilon_k/\varepsilon + 2)^n
\leq (1/c + 2)^n$ boxes of side $\varepsilon$, and conversely, so $N(\varepsilon_k) \leq (1/c + 2)^nN(\varepsilon)$ and $N(\varepsilon) \leq
(1/c + 2)^nN(\varepsilon_{k + 1})$. Hence
$$
\frac{\log N(\varepsilon_k) - C}{\log(1/\varepsilon_{k + 1})} \leq \frac{\log N(\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\varepsilon)} \leq \frac{\log
N(\varepsilon_{k + 1}) + C}{\log(1/\varepsilon_k)} ,
$$
with $C = n\log(1/c + 2)$. Since $\log(1/\varepsilon_{k + 1})/\log(1/\varepsilon_k) = (k + 1)/k \to 1$, the bounds have the same
$\liminf$ and $\limsup$ as the sequence.

## Python

Check on the Cantor set of generation $12$: the ratio $N(\varepsilon)/N(\varepsilon_k)$ for $\varepsilon$ between $\varepsilon_{k + 1} =
3^{-(k + 1)}$ and $\varepsilon_k = 3^{-k}$ stays bounded.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import CantorSetSystem
left = simulate(CantorSetSystem(), until=12).structures[-1]["cantor"].matrices[:, 0, 2]
def boxes(eps):
    return np.unique(np.concatenate([np.floor(left / eps), np.floor((left + 3.0**-12) / eps)])).size
ratios = [boxes(3.0**-k * f) / boxes(3.0**-k) for k in range(2, 9) for f in (1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4)]
print(f"ratios between {min(ratios):.3f} and {max(ratios):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
ratios between 1.000 and 1.737
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise makes the count of @exm-box-cantor exact. It counts the boxes of side $3^{-k}$ that meet the Cantor set,
using the closed intervals of generation $k$.

::: {#exr-box-cantor-count}
#### The count of the Cantor set

Prove that $N(3^{-k}) = 2^{k + 1}$ for the middle-thirds Cantor set $\mathcal C$, and check it for $k \leq 8$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathcal C$ is contained in the union of the $2^k$ intervals $[a, a + 3^{-k}]$ of generation $k$, whose left endpoints $a$ are
multiples of $3^{-k}$; both endpoints of every interval belong to $\mathcal C$, since they are never removed. The interval meets exactly
the two boxes $[a, a + 3^{-k})$ and $[a + 3^{-k}, a + 2 \cdot 3^{-k})$, the second through its right endpoint. Two intervals of
generation $k$ are separated by a gap of length at least $3^{-k}$, so the next interval starts at $a + 2 \cdot 3^{-k}$ or later, and the
$2^{k + 1}$ boxes are distinct. Hence $N(3^{-k}) = 2^{k + 1}$, between the bounds of @exm-box-cantor, and $\log N(3^{-k})/\log 3^k \to
\log 2/\log 3$.

## Python

The endpoints of generation $k$, exactly as fractions, and the number of distinct boxes $\lfloor x 3^k\rfloor$ they occupy.

```{.python .run}
from fractions import Fraction
left = [Fraction(0)]
for k in range(1, 9):
    left = [a / 3 for a in left] + [a / 3 + Fraction(2, 3) for a in left]
    ends = left + [a + Fraction(1, 3**k) for a in left]
    print(k, 2**k, len({int(x * 3**k) for x in ends}), 2 ** (k + 1))
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 2 4 4
2 4 8 8
3 8 16 16
4 16 32 32
5 32 64 64
6 64 128 128
7 128 256 256
8 256 512 512
```
::::
:::

Products of sets add dimensions, because a box of the product is a product of boxes. The fifth exercise proves this and builds a
Cantor dust in the plane.

::: {#exr-box-product}
#### Products add dimensions

Show that $N_{A \times B}(\varepsilon) = N_A(\varepsilon)N_B(\varepsilon)$ for the boxes of the definition, and hence that $D_0(A
\times B) = D_0(A) + D_0(B)$ when both exist. Check on $\mathcal C \times \mathcal C$, of dimension $2\log 2/\log 3 \approx 1.2619$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A box of $\mathbb R^{n + m}$ is a product $Q \times Q'$ of boxes of $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^m$, and it meets $A \times B$ exactly
when $Q$ meets $A$ and $Q'$ meets $B$. So the count multiplies, and $\log N_{A\times B}/\log(1/\varepsilon)$ is the sum of the two
ratios, which converge. (For lower and upper dimensions one only gets $\underline D_0(A) + \underline D_0(B) \leq \underline D_0(A
\times B)$ and the reverse inequality for upper dimensions.) The product $\mathcal C \times \mathcal C$ has the same dimension as the Koch
curve, but it is totally disconnected.

## Python

The endpoints of generation $9$ give a grid picture of $\mathcal C \times \mathcal C$ at resolution $3^{-9}$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import CantorSetSystem
left = np.rint(simulate(CantorSetSystem(), until=9).structures[-1]["cantor"].matrices[:, 0, 2] * 3**9).astype(int)
row = np.zeros(3**9, dtype=bool)
row[left] = True
dust = np.outer(row, row)
result = scaling(dust, kind="box-counting", scales=[3, 9, 27, 81, 243])
print("counts:", result.counts.astype(int).tolist(), f"slope {result.exponent:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
counts: [65536, 16384, 4096, 1024, 256] slope 1.2619
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise turns to the length of the Koch curve. Charbonneau notes that a seed of $5$ cm grown for $100$ generations
would wrap around the Earth thousands of times [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 3.5, eq. (3.1)].

::: {#exr-box-koch-length}
#### How long is the Koch curve?

Show that generation $k$ of the Koch curve has length $(4/3)^k$, that measured with yardstick $3^{-k}$ the limit curve has length
$\varepsilon^{1 - D_0}$ with $D_0 = \log 4/\log 3$, and compute how many times the curve of generation $100$ grown from $5$ cm would wrap
around the Earth (circumference $40\,075$ km).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each generation multiplies the number of segments by $4$ and their length by $\frac13$, so the length is $4^k3^{-k}$. With $\varepsilon
= 3^{-k}$, $(4/3)^k = 4^k\varepsilon = \varepsilon^{-\log 4/\log 3}\varepsilon = \varepsilon^{1 - D_0}$, as in
@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018 [eq. (3.52)]. The curve of generation $100$ has length $0.05\,(4/3)^{100}$ m.

## Python

The lengths that `KochCurveSystem` reports, and the number of turns around the Earth.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import KochCurveSystem
print("lengths:", simulate(KochCurveSystem(), until=6).get_values("koch.length").round(3).tolist())
print(f"turns around the Earth: {0.05 * (4 / 3) ** 100 / 40075e3:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lengths: [1.0, 1.333, 1.778, 2.37, 3.16, 4.214, 5.619]
turns around the Earth: 3890
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise makes @exm-box-harmonic-sequence precise. It shows by explicit bounds that a countable set can have box-counting
dimension one half.

::: {#exr-box-harmonic}
#### The dimension of $\{1/j\}$

For $A = \{1/j : j \geq 1\} \cup \{0\}$ and $0 < \varepsilon < \frac14$, let $m = \lceil\varepsilon^{-1/2}\rceil$. Show that
$\frac12\varepsilon^{-1/2} - 1 \leq N(\varepsilon) \leq 2\varepsilon^{-1/2} + 3$, and hence $D_0(A) = \frac12$. Compute
$N(\varepsilon)$ for $\varepsilon = 10^{-2}, \dots, 10^{-6}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Upper bound: the points $1/j$ with $j < m$ meet at most $m - 1 \leq \varepsilon^{-1/2}$ boxes; the others lie in $[0, 1/m] \subseteq [0,
\varepsilon^{1/2}]$, which meets at most $\varepsilon^{1/2}/\varepsilon + 1 = \varepsilon^{-1/2} + 1$ boxes. With the box of $0$ this
gives at most $2\varepsilon^{-1/2} + 3$. Lower bound: for $j(j + 1) \leq 1/\varepsilon$ consecutive points are at least $\varepsilon$
apart and lie in different boxes; this holds for $j \leq \varepsilon^{-1/2} - 1$, giving at least $\varepsilon^{-1/2} - 1 \geq
\frac12\varepsilon^{-1/2} - 1$ boxes. Both bounds are of order $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$.

## Python

The count of distinct boxes $\lfloor 1/(j\varepsilon)\rfloor$, with $j$ large enough that the remaining points fall in the box of $0$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
for e in range(2, 7):
    eps = 10.0**-e
    j = np.arange(1, int(10 / eps))
    n = np.unique(np.floor(1 / (j * eps))).size
    print(f"eps = 1e-{e}: N = {n}, N * sqrt(eps) = {n * np.sqrt(eps):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
eps = 1e-2: N = 20, N * sqrt(eps) = 2.000
eps = 1e-3: N = 63, N * sqrt(eps) = 1.992
eps = 1e-4: N = 200, N * sqrt(eps) = 2.000
eps = 1e-5: N = 632, N * sqrt(eps) = 1.999
eps = 1e-6: N = 2000, N * sqrt(eps) = 2.000
```
::::
:::

Smooth curves are one-dimensional, and so is the graph of any Lipschitz function. The eighth exercise proves this, which shows that a
fractal graph needs a function that is rough at every scale.

::: {#exr-box-lipschitz-graph}
#### Graphs of Lipschitz functions

Let $f : [0, 1] \to \mathbb R$ satisfy $\lvert f(x) - f(y)\rvert \leq L\lvert x - y\rvert$. Show that its graph has $N(\varepsilon) \leq
(L + 2)(1/\varepsilon + 1)$ and $D_0 = 1$. Count the boxes of the graph of $\sin(5x)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Over a column $[k\varepsilon, (k + 1)\varepsilon)$ the function varies by at most $L\varepsilon$, so the graph meets at most $L + 2$ boxes of
that column. There are at most $1/\varepsilon + 1$ columns, which gives the upper bound; the projection onto the first axis gives
$N(\varepsilon) \geq 1/\varepsilon$. So $D_0 = 1$.

## Python

The graph of $\sin(5x)$ ($L = 5$) sampled densely; the ratio $N(\varepsilon)\varepsilon$ stays between $1$ and $L + 2$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 400001)
y = np.sin(5 * x)
for eps in (1 / 16, 1 / 128, 1 / 1024):
    n = len(set(zip(np.floor(x / eps).astype(int), np.floor(y / eps).astype(int))))
    print(f"1/eps = {round(1 / eps)}: N = {n}, N * eps = {n * eps:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1/eps = 16: N = 63, N * eps = 3.938
1/eps = 128: N = 516, N * eps = 4.031
1/eps = 1024: N = 4113, N * eps = 4.017
```
::::
:::

Measured sets are finite, and a finite set has dimension zero. The ninth exercise shows how this appears in a box count of a chaos-game
sample of the gasket, and why only an intermediate range of scales is fitted [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 3.5,
Fig. 3.11].

::: {#exr-box-finite-sample}
#### Where a sample stops being fractal

Draw $m$ points of the gasket with `ChaosGameSystem` and compute the local slopes $\log(N(\varepsilon)/N(\varepsilon/2))/\log 2$ for
$\varepsilon = 2^{-1}, \dots, 2^{-10}$. Explain why they fall from $\log 3/\log 2$ towards $0$ at small $\varepsilon$, and estimate the
scale where this happens.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

At scale $2^{-k}$ the gasket meets of order $3^k$ boxes, and $m$ points can fill at most $m$ of them, so the count saturates once $3^k$
is comparable with $m$, that is below $\varepsilon^* \approx m^{-\log 2/\log 3}$. For $m = 20\,000$ this is $2^{-k^*}$ with $k^* = \log
m/\log 3 \approx 9$; the slopes are close to $1.585$ for $k$ up to about $6$ and then fall towards $0$.

## Python

Local slopes from a sample of $20\,000$ points after $25$ steps of the chaos game.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import ChaosGameSystem
points = simulate(ChaosGameSystem(n_points=20000, random_state=3), until=25, random_state=3).get_values("points.p")[-1]
counts = [len(set(map(tuple, np.floor(points * 2**k).astype(int)))) for k in range(1, 12)]
print("local slopes:", np.round(np.log2(np.array(counts[1:]) / counts[:-1]), 3).tolist())
```

```{.text .run-output}
local slopes: [1.585, 1.585, 1.585, 1.585, 1.585, 1.579, 1.39, 0.839, 0.36, 0.129]
```
::::
:::

The last exercise compares the box-counting dimension of the Hénon attractor with a dimension computed from the dynamics alone. The
Kaplan-Yorke dimension $D_L = k + \sum_{i \leq k}\lambda_{L,i}/\lvert\lambda_{L,k + 1}\rvert$, with $k$ the largest index whose partial
sum of exponents is positive, is conjectured to equal the information dimension [@datserisNonlinearDynamicsConcise2022, Sec.
5.4.4, eq. (5.9)].

::: {#exr-box-kaplan-yorke}
#### The Kaplan-Yorke dimension of the Hénon attractor

Compute the Lyapunov spectrum of the Hénon map at $a = 1.4$, $b = 0.3$ (@def-lyapunov-spectrum) and its Kaplan-Yorke dimension, and
compare with the box-counting slope of @exm-box-henon. Use $\lambda_{L,1} + \lambda_{L,2} = \log b$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Here $k = 1$ and $D_L = 1 + \lambda_{L,1}/\lvert\lambda_{L,2}\rvert$. Since the Jacobian has determinant $-b$, the exponents sum to $\log
0.3 \approx -1.204$ (@prp-volume-contraction), so with $\lambda_{L,1} \approx 0.42$ one gets $\lambda_{L,2} \approx -1.62$ and $D_L
\approx 1.26$, the value of the box count.

## Python

The spectrum from `lyapunov` and the dimension.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.core.analysis import lyapunov
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.dynamical_systems import HenonMapSystem
spectrum = lyapunov(HenonMapSystem(x=0.0, y=0.0), until=100000, transient=1000).exponents
print(f"spectrum {spectrum.round(4).tolist()}, sum {spectrum.sum():.4f}, D_L = {1 + spectrum[0] / abs(spectrum[1]):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
spectrum [0.4204, -1.6243], sum -1.2040, D_L = 1.2588
```
::::
:::
::::

### Self-similar sets

The Cantor set, the Koch curve and the gasket are each a union of smaller copies of themselves. Such a set is the fixed point of
a finite family of contracting similarities, an iterated function system, and the chaos game of
@dilaoDynamicalSystemChaos2023 [Sec. 5.4] draws it by applying the maps at random to a point. The theorem says that the copies
determine the dimension: if they do not overlap too much, $D_0$ is the exponent $s$ for which the copies, measured as $r_i^s$, add
up to the whole. The condition on the overlaps is the open set condition; without it the copies can pile up and the dimension can
be smaller. A similarity of ratio $r_i$ is a map with $\lVert T_i(\mathbf x) - T_i(\mathbf y)\rVert = r_i\lVert\mathbf x - \mathbf
y\rVert$; the ratios always carry their index, unlike the logistic parameter $r$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-similarity-dimension}
#### Dimension of self-similar sets

Let $T_1, \dots, T_m : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^n$, $m \geq 2$, be similarities with ratios $0 < r_i < 1$.

(a) There is exactly one nonempty compact set $A$ with $A = T_1(A) \cup \dots \cup T_m(A)$, the **attractor** of the iterated function
system, and $A$ is called **self-similar**.

(b) The equation $\sum_{i = 1}^m r_i^s = 1$ has exactly one solution $s = D_s > 0$, the **similarity dimension**, and $\overline
D_0(A) \leq D_s$.

(c) If the system satisfies the **open set condition**, that is, there is a nonempty bounded open set $V$ with $T_i(V) \subseteq V$
for all $i$ and $T_i(V) \cap T_j(V) = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$, then the box-counting dimension of $A$ exists and $D_0(A) = D_s$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) The nonempty compact subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ form a complete metric space under the Hausdorff distance $d_H(E, F)$, the
least $\delta$ such that each set lies within $\delta$ of the other [@dilaoDynamicalSystemChaos2023, Sec. 5.4]. The map $\mathcal
T(E) = \bigcup_iT_i(E)$ sends compact sets to compact sets, and $d_H(\mathcal T(E), \mathcal T(F)) \leq \max_ir_i\,d_H(E, F)$, since
$T_i(E)$ lies within $r_i\delta$ of $T_i(F)$ when $E$ lies within $\delta$ of $F$. By the contraction mapping theorem
([`thm-contraction-mapping`](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/sets-relations-topology/index.qmd#thm-contraction-mapping))
$\mathcal T$ has exactly one fixed point $A$, and $\mathcal T^k(E) \to A$ for every nonempty compact $E$.

(b) The function $\phi(s) = \sum_ir_i^s$ is continuous and strictly decreasing, with $\phi(0) = m \geq 2$ and $\phi(s) \to 0$, so it
takes the value $1$ exactly once. For a word $w = i_1\dots i_k$ write $T_w = T_{i_1} \circ \dots \circ T_{i_k}$ and $r_w = r_{i_1}\cdots
r_{i_k}$ ($r_\varnothing = 1$), and let $r_{\min} = \min_ir_i$. For $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, let $W_\varepsilon$ be the set of words with
$r_w \leq \varepsilon < r_{w^-}$, where $w^-$ is $w$ without its last letter. Starting from the empty word and replacing every word $w$
with $r_w > \varepsilon$ by its $m$ children $wi$ produces $W_\varepsilon$ after finitely many steps. A replacement keeps both
$\bigcup_wT_w(A) = A$ (because $T_w(A) = \bigcup_iT_{wi}(A)$) and $\sum_wr_w^s = 1$ for $s = D_s$ (because $\sum_ir_{wi}^s = r_w^s\phi(D_s)$).
So
$$
A = \bigcup_{w \in W_\varepsilon}T_w(A) ,\qquad \sum_{w \in W_\varepsilon}r_w^{D_s} = 1 ,\qquad r_{\min}\varepsilon < r_w \leq \varepsilon
\quad (w \in W_\varepsilon) .
$$
The second and third facts give $\lvert W_\varepsilon\rvert(r_{\min}\varepsilon)^{D_s} < 1$. Let $d$ be the diameter of $A$. Each
$T_w(A)$ has diameter $r_wd \leq \varepsilon d$, so it lies in a cube of side $\varepsilon d$ and meets at most $2^n$ boxes of side
$\varepsilon d$. Hence
$$
N(\varepsilon d) \leq 2^n\lvert W_\varepsilon\rvert < 2^nr_{\min}^{-D_s}\varepsilon^{-D_s} ,
$$
and $\overline D_0(A) \leq D_s$ (the factor $d$ does not change the limits, by @exr-box-geometric-scales).

(c) First, $A \subseteq \bar V$: the closure $\bar V$ is compact and $\mathcal T(\bar V) \subseteq \bar V$, so the sets $\mathcal T^k(\bar
V)$ are compact subsets of $\bar V$ converging to $A$. Next, the open sets $T_w(V)$, $w \in W_\varepsilon$, are pairwise disjoint: two
distinct words of $W_\varepsilon$ are not prefixes of one another, so they read $uiv$ and $ujv'$ with $i \neq j$, and $T_{uiv}(V)
\subseteq T_u(T_i(V))$ and $T_{ujv'}(V) \subseteq T_u(T_j(V))$ are disjoint because $T_u$ is injective. Choose a ball of radius $a$ in
$V$ and a radius $b$ with $V$ inside a ball of radius $b$. Then $T_w(V)$ contains a ball of radius $r_wa > r_{\min}a\varepsilon$ and has
diameter at most $2r_wb \leq 2b\varepsilon$.

Fix a box $Q$ of side $\varepsilon$. If $T_w(\bar V)$ meets $Q$, then $T_w(V)$ lies within the ball of radius $(\sqrt n + 2b)\varepsilon$
around the centre of $Q$. Disjoint sets each containing a ball of radius $r_{\min}a\varepsilon$ fit in this ball at most $q = ((\sqrt n
+ 2b)/(r_{\min}a))^n$ times, by comparing volumes. Now take the $N(\varepsilon)$ boxes that meet $A$. For each $w \in W_\varepsilon$, the
nonempty set $T_w(A) \subseteq A \cap T_w(\bar V)$ meets one of these boxes, and each box is met in this way by at most $q$ words. Hence
$\lvert W_\varepsilon\rvert \leq qN(\varepsilon)$. Since $r_w \leq \varepsilon$ and $\sum_wr_w^{D_s} = 1$, also $\lvert W_\varepsilon\rvert
\geq \varepsilon^{-D_s}$, so $N(\varepsilon) \geq \varepsilon^{-D_s}/q$ and $\underline D_0(A) \geq D_s$. With (b), $D_0(A)$ exists and equals
$D_s$. $\square$

The open set condition also bounds the dimension by that of the space: the disjoint sets $T_i(V) \subseteq V$ have volumes
$r_i^n\operatorname{vol}(V)$, so $\sum_ir_i^n \leq 1$ and $D_s \leq n$. The proof follows the standard argument for box dimensions; the
same value is the Hausdorff dimension, a theorem of Moran and Hutchinson that is not needed here.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The middle-thirds Cantor set is the attractor of two maps. The theorem recovers the dimension computed directly in
@exr-box-cantor-count.

::: {#exm-similarity-cantor}
#### The Cantor set as an attractor

$T_1(x) = x/3$ and $T_2(x) = x/3 + \frac23$ map $[0, 1]$ onto its outer thirds, so the Cantor set $\mathcal C$ satisfies $\mathcal C =
T_1(\mathcal C) \cup T_2(\mathcal C)$. The open interval $V = (0, 1)$ satisfies the open set condition, and $2\cdot3^{-s} = 1$ gives
$D_0 = \log 2/\log 3$ [@dilaoDynamicalSystemChaos2023, Example 5.8].
:::

The Koch curve needs four maps of ratio $\frac13$: two of them are rotations by $\pm60°$ combined with a contraction. The theorem gives
the value that the local slopes of @exm-box-koch approach.

::: {#exm-similarity-koch}
#### The Koch curve

The four maps send the segment $[0, 1]$ onto the four segments of generation one; the open set condition holds with $V$ the interior of
the isosceles triangle with base $[0, 1]$ and apex $(\frac12, \frac{\sqrt3}6)$. So $4\cdot3^{-s} = 1$ and $D_0 = \log 4/\log 3 \approx
1.2619$, the "funny" dimension of @thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018 [eq. (3.50)].
:::

The gasket is the attractor of the three maps of @dilaoDynamicalSystemChaos2023 [Example 5.9], which halve the plane towards three
corners. The open interior of the triangle is the set $V$.

::: {#exm-similarity-gasket}
#### The Sierpiński gasket

$T_1(x, y) = \frac12(x, y)$, $T_2(x, y) = \frac12(x + 1, y)$ and $T_3(x, y) = \frac12(x + \frac12, y + 1)$ have the triangle with
vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(\frac12, 1)$ as attractor of their filled version and the gasket as attractor. $3\cdot2^{-s} = 1$ gives
$D_0 = \log 3/\log 2 \approx 1.585$; the box counts of @exm-box-sierpinski and @exr-box-finite-sample approach it.
:::

The Sierpiński carpet keeps eight of the nine squares of a third of the side. It is the analogue of the gasket for squares, and its
dimension is close to $2$.

::: {#exm-similarity-carpet}
#### The Sierpiński carpet

Eight maps of ratio $\frac13$, with $V$ the open unit square, give $8\cdot3^{-s} = 1$ and $D_0 = \log 8/\log 3 \approx 1.8928$.
`SierpinskiSubstitutionSystem` draws it with `shape="carpet"`; generation $k$ has $8^k$ squares of area $9^{-k}$, so its area tends
to $0$.
:::

The ratios need not be equal. With two pieces of ratios $\frac14$ and $\frac12$ the equation of part (b) is a quadratic, and the
dimension is a logarithm of the golden ratio.

::: {#exm-similarity-unequal}
#### Unequal ratios

$T_1(x) = x/4$ and $T_2(x) = x/2 + \frac12$ satisfy the open set condition with $V = (0, 1)$. With $u = 2^{-s}$ the equation $4^{-s} +
2^{-s} = 1$ reads $u^2 + u = 1$, so $u = (\sqrt5 - 1)/2 = 1/\varphi$ and $D_0 = \log\varphi/\log 2 \approx 0.6942$, where $\varphi$ is
the golden ratio.
:::

The theorem also covers sets that are not fractal. The interval is the union of its two halves, and the similarity dimension is the
ordinary one.

::: {#exm-similarity-interval}
#### The interval and the square

$x \mapsto x/2$ and $x \mapsto x/2 + \frac12$ have attractor $[0, 1]$ and $2\cdot2^{-s} = 1$ gives $s = 1$; the four quarter-squares of the
unit square give $4\cdot2^{-s} = 1$, $s = 2$. The halves overlap only in their boundaries, so the open interiors satisfy the open set
condition.
:::

Without the open set condition the similarity dimension can exceed the box-counting dimension, and even the dimension of the space.
Three maps of ratio $\frac12$ that pile up on the interval show this.

::: {#exm-similarity-overlap}
#### When copies overlap

$T_1(x) = x/2$, $T_2(x) = x/2 + \frac14$ and $T_3(x) = x/2 + \frac12$ map $[0, 1]$ into itself and their images cover it, so the attractor
is $[0, 1]$, of dimension $1$. But $3\cdot2^{-s} = 1$ gives $D_s = \log 3/\log 2 \approx 1.585 > 1$: only the inequality of part (b)
holds, and the open set condition must fail.
:::

The chaos game draws the attractor of any iterated function system, not only of similarities. The Barnsley fern is the attractor of four
affine maps, each picked with its own probability; the theorem does not apply, but the box count does.

::: {#exm-similarity-fern}
#### The Barnsley fern

`ChaosGameSystem("barnsley")` iterates the four affine maps of the fern on $20\,000$ points. The maps are not similarities, so no
formula gives the dimension, and the box count of the cloud gives its slope over the scales where the sample is dense enough.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import ChaosGameSystem
points = simulate(ChaosGameSystem("barnsley", n_points=20000, random_state=5), until=40, random_state=5).get_values("points.p")[-1]
lo, hi = points.min(axis=0), points.max(axis=0)
side = (hi - lo).max()
grid = np.histogram2d(*(points - lo).T / side, bins=512, range=[[0, 1], [0, 1]])[0] > 0
result = scaling(grid, kind="box-counting", scales=[4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
print("boxes:", result.counts.astype(int).tolist(), f"slope {result.exponent:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
boxes: [3521, 1109, 318, 92, 27] slope 1.765
```
:::

The chaos game converges because the maps contract. A point that has been mapped $k$ times lies within $(\max_ir_i)^k\operatorname{diam}$
of the attractor, wherever it started, which is part (a) of the theorem seen from one orbit.

::: {#exm-similarity-chaos-game}
#### Convergence of the chaos game

For the gasket the distance to $A$ halves at every step, so after $25$ steps the $20\,000$ points of `ChaosGameSystem` lie within
$2^{-25}$ of the gasket; the initial points, spread over the unit square, are forgotten after a few steps, which @fig-koch-sierpinski
shows.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import ChaosGameSystem
cloud = simulate(ChaosGameSystem(n_points=20000, random_state=1), until=25, random_state=1).get_values("points.p")
for step in (0, 1, 2, 5, 25):
    x, y = cloud[step].T
    inside = (y >= 0) & (y <= 2 * x + 1e-9) & (y <= 2 * (1 - x) + 1e-9)
    print(f"step {step}: share in the triangle {inside.mean():.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
step 0: share in the triangle 0.503
step 1: share in the triangle 0.667
step 2: share in the triangle 0.778
step 5: share in the triangle 0.935
step 25: share in the triangle 1.000
```
:::

Self-similarity in nature is statistical rather than exact. A chaotic attractor is self-similar only in a qualitative sense, because the
map transforms different parts of the state space differently [@datserisNonlinearDynamicsConcise2022, Sec. 5.3.2]; the theorem is the
exact model against which such sets are compared.

::: {#exm-similarity-statistical}
#### Exact and statistical self-similarity

Zooming into the Koch curve by a factor $27$ reproduces generation three exactly [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Fig. 3.6],
whereas zooming into the Hénon attractor of @fig-henon-attractor reproduces bundles of curves that look alike but are never identical.
For such sets the dimension is measured, as in @exm-box-henon, not computed from ratios.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise solves the equation of part (b) numerically for the examples above. It is the computation that turns a construction
into a dimension.

::: {#exr-similarity-solve}
#### Solving for the similarity dimension

Solve $\sum_ir_i^s = 1$ for the Cantor set, the Koch curve, the gasket, the carpet and the ratios $(\frac14, \frac12)$, and compare with
the closed forms.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

For $m$ equal ratios $r$, $mr^s = 1$ gives $s = \log m/\log(1/r)$: $\log 2/\log 3$, $\log 4/\log 3$, $\log 3/\log 2$ and $\log 8/\log 3$.
The unequal pair gives $\log\varphi/\log 2$ (@exm-similarity-unequal). Since $\phi$ is decreasing, bisection or Brent's method finds the
root between $0$ and the dimension of the space.

## Python

Brent's method on $\phi(s) - 1$.

```{.python .run}
import math
from scipy.optimize import brentq
systems = {"Cantor": [1 / 3] * 2, "Koch": [1 / 3] * 4, "gasket": [1 / 2] * 3, "carpet": [1 / 3] * 8, "1/4, 1/2": [1 / 4, 1 / 2]}
closed = [math.log(2, 3), math.log(4, 3), math.log(3, 2), math.log(8, 3), math.log((1 + 5**0.5) / 2, 2)]
for (name, ratios), exact in zip(systems.items(), closed):
    s = brentq(lambda s: sum(r**s for r in ratios) - 1, 1e-9, 3)
    print(f"{name}: {s:.6f} (closed form {exact:.6f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
Cantor: 0.630930 (closed form 0.630930)
Koch: 1.261860 (closed form 1.261860)
gasket: 1.584963 (closed form 1.584963)
carpet: 1.892789 (closed form 1.892789)
1/4, 1/2: 0.694242 (closed form 0.694242)
```
::::
:::

The proof of part (b) rests on the cut sets $W_\varepsilon$. The second exercise checks their two properties on the unequal ratios.

::: {#exr-similarity-cut}
#### The cut sets

For the ratios $(\frac14, \frac12)$, list the words of $W_\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon = 2^{-k}$, $k = 1, \dots, 12$, and verify that
$\sum_wr_w^{D_s} = 1$ and $\lvert W_\varepsilon\rvert(r_{\min}\varepsilon)^{D_s} < 1 \leq \lvert W_\varepsilon\rvert\varepsilon^{D_s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The construction of the proof refines words until $r_w \leq \varepsilon$. Each refinement preserves $\sum r_w^{D_s}$, which starts at $1$,
and the bounds follow from $r_{\min}\varepsilon < r_w \leq \varepsilon$. With $D_s = \log\varphi/\log 2$, $\lvert W_\varepsilon\rvert$
grows like $\varepsilon^{-D_s}$; here it is a Fibonacci number, since a word of ratio $2^{-k}$ ends either in a letter of ratio
$\frac12$ or of ratio $\frac14$.

## Python

The cut sets by refinement, with the two checks.

```{.python .run}
import math
ratios, s = [0.25, 0.5], math.log((1 + 5**0.5) / 2, 2)
for k in range(1, 13):
    eps, words, cut = 2.0**-k, [1.0], []
    while words:
        r = words.pop()
        if r <= eps:
            cut.append(r)
        else:
            words += [r * q for q in ratios]
    total = sum(r**s for r in cut)
    print(k, len(cut), round(total, 12), len(cut) * (0.25 * eps) ** s < 1 <= len(cut) * eps**s + 1e-12)
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 2 1.0 True
2 3 1.0 True
3 5 1.0 True
4 8 1.0 True
5 13 1.0 True
6 21 1.0 True
7 34 1.0 True
8 55 1.0 True
9 89 1.0 True
10 144 1.0 True
11 233 1.0 True
12 377 1.0 True
```
::::
:::

The third exercise proves the remark after the theorem: under the open set condition the similarity dimension cannot exceed the dimension
of the space. It explains why the overlapping maps of @exm-similarity-overlap must violate the condition.

::: {#exr-similarity-volume-bound}
#### A volume bound

Show that the open set condition implies $\sum_ir_i^n \leq 1$, hence $D_s \leq n$. Deduce that no open set $V$ works for the three maps
of @exm-similarity-overlap, and compute $\sum_ir_i^n$ for the examples of the unit.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A similarity of ratio $r_i$ multiplies volumes by $r_i^n$. The sets $T_i(V)$ are disjoint subsets of $V$, so $\sum_ir_i^n\operatorname{vol}(V)
\leq \operatorname{vol}(V)$, with $\operatorname{vol}(V) > 0$ because $V$ is open and nonempty. Since $\phi$ is decreasing, $\phi(n) \leq 1 =
\phi(D_s)$ gives $D_s \leq n$. For the overlapping maps, $n = 1$ and $\sum r_i = \frac32 > 1$, so no such $V$ exists.

## Python

The sums $\sum_ir_i^n$ in the dimension $n$ of the space.

```{.python .run}
cases = {"Cantor (n = 1)": ([1 / 3] * 2, 1), "Koch (n = 2)": ([1 / 3] * 4, 2), "gasket (n = 2)": ([1 / 2] * 3, 2),
         "carpet (n = 2)": ([1 / 3] * 8, 2), "overlap (n = 1)": ([1 / 2] * 3, 1)}
for name, (ratios, n) in cases.items():
    print(f"{name}: sum r_i^n = {sum(r**n for r in ratios):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
Cantor (n = 1): sum r_i^n = 0.6667
Koch (n = 2): sum r_i^n = 0.4444
gasket (n = 2): sum r_i^n = 0.7500
carpet (n = 2): sum r_i^n = 0.8889
overlap (n = 1): sum r_i^n = 1.5000
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise checks the unequal ratios of @exm-similarity-unequal by playing the chaos game on the line. A cloud of points iterated
by the two maps fills the attractor, and its box count should give $\log\varphi/\log 2$.

::: {#exr-similarity-unequal-game}
#### A chaos game on the line

Run `ChaosGameSystem` with the maps $x \mapsto x/4$ and $x \mapsto x/2 + \frac12$ (acting on the first coordinate, with $y \mapsto 0$),
weighted $\frac14$ and $\frac12$ in proportion to the lengths, and fit the box-counting slope.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By the theorem the attractor has $D_0 = \log\varphi/\log 2 \approx 0.694$. The weights only change how often each part is visited; weights
proportional to $r_i^{D_s}$ would spread the points most evenly, and any positive weights give the same support.

## Python

Affine maps $(a, b, c, d, e, f)$ act as $(x, y) \mapsto (ax + by + e, cx + dy + f)$; here $y$ is sent to $0$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import ChaosGameSystem
game = ChaosGameSystem(maps=[(0.25, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0), (0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 0)], weights=[1, 2], n_points=50000, random_state=4)
x = simulate(game, until=40, random_state=4).get_values("points.p")[-1][:, 0]
line = np.zeros(2**16, dtype=bool)
line[np.minimum((x * 2**16).astype(int), 2**16 - 1)] = True
result = scaling(line, kind="box-counting", scales=[2**k for k in range(4, 12)])
print(f"slope {result.exponent:.4f}, log(phi)/log 2 = {np.log((1 + 5**0.5) / 2) / np.log(2):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
slope 0.6941, log(phi)/log 2 = 0.6942
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise looks at the overlapping system of @exm-similarity-overlap through the chaos game. The copies pile up, and the
cloud fills an interval.

::: {#exr-similarity-overlap-game}
#### Piled-up copies

Play the chaos game with the three maps of @exm-similarity-overlap and show that the box count gives $D_0 = 1$, not $\log 3/\log 2$.
Show also that the attractor is $[0, 1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$T_1([0, 1]) \cup T_2([0, 1]) \cup T_3([0, 1]) = [0, \frac12] \cup [\frac14, \frac34] \cup [\frac12, 1] = [0, 1]$, so $[0, 1]$ is a fixed
point of $\mathcal T$ and, by uniqueness, the attractor. Its dimension is $1 < \log 3/\log 2$, the strict inequality allowed by part (b).

## Python

The occupied boxes of $50\,000$ points on a line of $2^{16}$ cells.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import ChaosGameSystem
maps = [(0.5, 0, 0, 0, shift, 0) for shift in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5)]
x = simulate(ChaosGameSystem(maps=maps, n_points=50000, random_state=6), until=40, random_state=6).get_values("points.p")[-1][:, 0]
line = np.zeros(2**16, dtype=bool)
line[np.minimum((x * 2**16).astype(int), 2**16 - 1)] = True
result = scaling(line, kind="box-counting", scales=[2**k for k in range(6, 12)])
print(f"range [{x.min():.4f}, {x.max():.4f}], slope {result.exponent:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
range [0.0002, 0.9993], slope 0.9996
```
::::
:::

Four maps of ratio $\frac13$ towards the corners of the square give a Cantor dust. The sixth exercise identifies it with the product of
@exr-box-product and checks the dimension with the chaos game.

::: {#exr-similarity-dust}
#### The Cantor dust

Show that the attractor of the four maps $(x, y) \mapsto \frac13(x, y) + \frac23(i, j)$, $i, j \in \{0, 1\}$, is $\mathcal C \times
\mathcal C$, and that the theorem and @exr-box-product give the same dimension. Estimate it with `ChaosGameSystem`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathcal C \times \mathcal C = (T_1(\mathcal C) \cup T_2(\mathcal C)) \times (T_1(\mathcal C) \cup T_2(\mathcal C))$ is the union of the
four products $T_i(\mathcal C) \times T_j(\mathcal C)$, which are the images of $\mathcal C \times \mathcal C$ under the four maps; by
uniqueness it is the attractor. The theorem gives $4\cdot3^{-s} = 1$, $s = \log 4/\log 3 = 2\log 2/\log 3$, the sum of the two
dimensions.

## Python

Box counting of a chaos-game sample on a grid of $3^6$ cells.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import ChaosGameSystem
maps = [(1 / 3, 0, 0, 1 / 3, 2 * i / 3, 2 * j / 3) for i in (0, 1) for j in (0, 1)]
points = simulate(ChaosGameSystem(maps=maps, n_points=40000, random_state=7), until=30, random_state=7).get_values("points.p")[-1]
grid = np.histogram2d(*points.T, bins=729, range=[[0, 1], [0, 1]])[0] > 0
result = scaling(grid, kind="box-counting", scales=[3, 9, 27, 81])
print("boxes:", result.counts.astype(int).tolist(), f"slope {result.exponent:.4f}, log 4 / log 3 = {np.log(4) / np.log(3):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
boxes: [1024, 256, 64, 16] slope 1.2619, log 4 / log 3 = 1.2619
```
::::
:::

The carpet of @exm-similarity-carpet is drawn by substitution rather than by the chaos game. The seventh exercise measures its dimension
on the polygons of generation five.

::: {#exr-similarity-carpet}
#### The dimension of the carpet

Rasterise generation $5$ of the Sierpiński carpet on a grid of $3^6$ cells and fit the box-counting slope over boxes of $3, 9, 27$ and $81$
cells. Explain why the counts are exact powers of $8$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With the grid aligned to the construction, a box of side $3^{-j}$ for $j \leq 5$ is either a square of generation $j$ or one of the removed
squares, so $N(3^{-j}) = 8^j$ and every local slope is $\log 8/\log 3$. Only boundary cells between filled and removed squares could add
to the count, and the alignment avoids them.

## Python

The carpet on a grid of $729$ cells.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import SierpinskiSubstitutionSystem
carpet = simulate(SierpinskiSubstitutionSystem("carpet"), until=5).structures[-1]["sierpinski"]
result = scaling(carpet.get_raster(729), kind="box-counting", scales=[3, 9, 27, 81])
print("boxes:", result.counts.astype(int).tolist(), f"slope {result.exponent:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
boxes: [32768, 4096, 512, 64] slope 1.8928
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise varies the ratio of a Cantor set. Keeping two outer pieces of ratio $r$ gives a whole family of dimensions between $0$
and $1$.

::: {#exr-similarity-cantor-ratio}
#### Cantor sets of any dimension

Show that the attractor of $x \mapsto rx$ and $x \mapsto rx + 1 - r$, $0 < r < \frac12$, has $D_0 = \log 2/\log(1/r)$, and find $r$ for
the dimensions $\frac14$, $\frac12$ and $\frac34$. Check $r = \frac14$ with `CantorSetSystem`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$V = (0, 1)$ satisfies the open set condition because the images $(0, r)$ and $(1 - r, 1)$ are disjoint for $r < \frac12$, and $2r^s = 1$
gives $s = \log 2/\log(1/r)$. Inverting, $r = 2^{-1/s}$: $r = \frac1{16}$, $\frac14$ and $2^{-4/3} \approx 0.397$.

## Python

Generation $8$ of the Cantor set of ratio $\frac14$, whose intervals have length $4^{-8}$; counting the intervals that each box of side
$4^{-j}$ meets is exact on the left endpoints.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import CantorSetSystem
trajectory = simulate(CantorSetSystem(ratio=0.25), until=8)
print("intervals:", int(trajectory.get_values("cantor.size")[-1]), "lengths:", trajectory.get_values("cantor.length")[-1].round(8))
left = trajectory.structures[-1]["cantor"].matrices[:, 0, 2]
counts = [np.unique(np.floor(left * 4**j + 1e-9)).size for j in range(1, 9)]
print("counts:", counts, "slope", round(scaling(np.column_stack([4.0 ** np.arange(1, 9), counts]), kind="allometric").exponent, 4))
```

```{.text .run-output}
intervals: 256 lengths: 0.00390625
counts: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256] slope 0.5
```

The ninth exercise designs a self-similar set of a prescribed dimension. Choosing eight of the sixteen squares of a $4 \times 4$ grid
gives a set of dimension exactly $\frac32$.

::: {#exr-similarity-design}
#### A set of dimension three halves

Show that the eight maps $(x, y) \mapsto \frac14(x, y) + \frac14(i, j)$ for the cells $(i, j)$ of a checkerboard pattern (with $i + j$ even)
have an attractor of dimension $\frac32$. Check it with the chaos game.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The eight images of the open unit square are distinct open cells of the $4 \times 4$ grid, so the open set condition holds, and $8\cdot4^{-s}
= 1$ gives $s = \log 8/\log 4 = \frac32$.

The chaos game with the eight maps, binned on $4^5$ cells.

The last exercise compares the bound of the proof with real counts. The constant $2^nr_{\min}^{-D_s}$ of part (b) is crude, and the exercise
shows by how much on the Koch curve.

::: {#exr-similarity-koch-bound}
#### The upper bound on the Koch curve

For the Koch curve, part (b) gives $N(3^{-k}) \leq 2^2\cdot3^{D_s}\cdot4^k = 16\cdot4^k$ with $d = 1$. Compare with the counts of
@exm-box-koch and compute $N(3^{-k})/4^k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $r_{\min} = \frac13$, $r_{\min}^{-D_s} = 3^{\log 4/\log 3} = 4$, so the bound is $2^2\cdot4\cdot\varepsilon^{-D_s}$; at $\varepsilon =
3^{-k}$, $\varepsilon^{-D_s} = 4^k$. The measured ratio $N/4^k$ settles near $1.2$, far below $16$: each copy of diameter $3^{-k}$ meets on
average only slightly more than one box.

## Python

The counts of generation $9$ at boxes of side $3^{-k}$, $k = 2, \dots, 7$.

```{.python .run}
import math
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals import KochCurveSystem
koch = simulate(KochCurveSystem(), until=9).structures[-1]["koch"]
result = scaling(koch.get_raster(6561, bounds=(0, 0, 1, 1)), kind="box-counting", scales=[3**j for j in range(1, 7)])
for side, n in zip(result.scales, result.counts):
    k = 8 - round(math.log(side, 3))
    print(f"k = {k}: N = {int(n)}, N / 4^k = {n / 4**k:.3f}, bound 16")
```

k = 5: N = 1233, N / 4^k = 1.204, bound 16
k = 4: N = 294, N / 4^k = 1.148, bound 16
k = 3: N = 67, N / 4^k = 1.047, bound 16
